BBC News

No cost of living payment for NI until Stormont budget agreed, says Bryant

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant said Stormont needed to agree its own budget

Chris Bryant is standing to the side, mouth open mid-talking. There are blurred trees and figures behind him. He is wearing a blue three-piece suit and red tie with white dots.

The secretary of state has warned that a cost of living payment cannot be made in Northern Ireland until an executive budget is agreed.

It comes after the Chancellor John Healey announced the £100 payment for households in England, based on how much council tax they pay.

Delivering his first Budget, Healey said money would be made available to Stormont to fund an equivalent scheme.

However Sir Chris Bryant said Stormont would not be in a legal position to deliver the money without a budget.

Seven months into the financial year the Northern Ireland Executive has still not agreed a budget.

Stormont ministers say the UK's devolution funding formula no longer delivers enough for them to produce a balanced budget.

Sir Chris has offered them an additional £525m this year but they said it is still inadequate.

Stormont ministers will have to agree a budget if they want to access the funds announced at the UK budget, but it is up to them if they wish to use that money for such an energy scheme.

Finance Minister John O'Dowd indicated his preference would be to fund an equivalent scheme, which would cost just under £90m.

The administrations in Scotland and Wales have said they intend to implement their own schemes.

Northern Ireland does not have council tax so another mechanism will have to be used to identify who gets the payment.

Stormont officials have recent experience of designing similar payments, such as the home heating oil voucher scheme.

Overall, Northern Ireland will get an additional £270m for public services as a result of the Budget, of which £131m can be used this year.

What can households in Northern Ireland expect?

All households can also expect to get further help with their electricity bills.

Last month, households in NI got £63 off their bill as the local outworking of two schemes which apply in Great Britain, which has a separately regulated electricity market.

Part of that discount related to a temporary VAT cut on bills in GB, which is being extended.

The Treasury said it was \"providing funding for the Northern Ireland Executive to provide comparable support with household electricity bills.\"

The intention is to apply the VAT cut in NI from April 2027, bringing it in line with the rest of the UK.

The government is also removing a 4% tariff, or import tax, on heating oil imported to NI from outside the EU.

EU produced heating oil is already zero tariff.

That moves potentially matters more in NI than other parts of the UK as oil is still the predominant heating fuel in NI.

However, in practice, it is likely to make little difference to consumer prices in the short term but could open up the market to wider sources of supply.

The government is also providing £1m for an investment summit in Northern Ireland to \"highlight Northern Ireland's potential as the only place in the world with dual access to the UK internal market and EU market\".

A similar event was held in Belfast in 2023.

There is also a £7.5m investment for Queen's University Centre for Secure Information Technologies (CSIT).

It is a centre of excellence in cyber security which has close links to the UK National Cyber Security Centre, a part of GCHQ.

John O'Dowd said the Budget would bring \"cold comfort to workers' families\"

Stormont gets a population-based share of additional spending allocated to public services in England.

Stormont's Department of Finance will make its own calculations of when that money can be spent and what it can be spent on.

Finance Minister John O'Dowd said the Budget would \"bring cold comfort to workers' families and indeed businesses out there who are struggling under a huge cost of living crisis\".

Addressing reporters, he said the package on offer was not enough to allow Stormont ministers to agree their own budget.

\"There remains a significant gap between the funding required by the executive to deliver front-line public services; pay our public sector workers the pay uplifts they deserve and grow our economy than that was put on the table today by the British government.\"

O'Dowd reiterated that compared to Scotland and Wales, Northern Ireland was funded below its level of need and he called for \"further engagement\" with Westminster on the issue.

Sir Chris Bryant says Stormont would not be in a legal position to deliver the money without a budget

Colin Neill, chief executive of Hospitality Ulster, said measures introduced to support hospitality elsewhere in the UK should generate additional funding for NI through the Barnett formula - the measure used to work out how much money the UK government sends to devolved nations each year.

\"It is essential that this money reaches our sector,\" Neill said.

\"The government cannot continue to raise wages without addressing the excessive taxation of the hospitality industry which is now over 40%.\"

Glyn Roberts, from Retail NI, said small businesses in Northern Ireland should be given the same support as their counterparts in England.

\"Our High Streets have the highest vacancy rates in the UK, at 25%.\"

He added that the executive must use the additional funding to \"prioritise small business rates relief, support independent retailers and help tackle the growing high street vacancy crisis\".

Leo Slevin was not impressed with the amount of financial help on energy costs
